subject: Svenska 3
title: Rhetorical analysis and argumentation
sourceSummary: In-depth analysis of argumentation with logical fallacies, assessing a text's credibility rhetorically, and how a sender adapts language to the recipient in complex texts.

questions.prompt: "You can't be right about climate policy, you're not even a scientist." What logical fallacy is this an example of?
questions.opener: Is the issue itself being attacked, or the person raising it?
choices: Straw man (distorting the opponent's position)
Ad hominem (a personal attack instead of addressing the issue)
Circular reasoning
False dichotomy
questions.explanation: Ad hominem means attacking the person putting forward an argument instead of addressing the argument itself — here the position is dismissed simply because the person lacks a certain title, which says nothing about whether the position is correct.

questions.prompt: "Either we commit fully to nuclear power, or the country will be left without electricity." Which logical fallacy is this claim built on?
questions.opener: Are there really only two possible outcomes here?
choices: Straw man
Argument from authority
False dichotomy (presenting only two extremes as the only alternatives)
Ad hominem
questions.explanation: A false dichotomy presents only two opposing alternatives as if they were the only possible ones, even though more nuanced alternatives exist (e.g. a combination of energy sources). It is neither a personal attack nor an argument from authority.

questions.prompt: A debater says: "My opponents apparently want us to close all schools entirely" — even though the opponents actually only proposed fewer administrative meetings. What is this logical fallacy called?
questions.opener: The position being addressed is heavily distorted compared with what was actually said.
choices: Straw man (distorting and exaggerating the opponent's position to make it easier to dismiss)
Circular reasoning
False dichotomy
Argument from authority
questions.explanation: A straw man is created by distorting or exaggerating the opponent's actual position into something easier to dismiss, and then addressing the distorted version rather than the real argument.

questions.prompt: Which of the following most strengthens a speaker's ETHOS in a debate about education policy?
questions.opener: Ethos is about the sender's credibility — what builds it?
choices: Speaking loudly and interrupting the opponent often
Avoiding mentioning any sources at all to appear more confident
Joking away difficult questions
Presenting relevant experience, referring to reliable sources, and addressing counterarguments objectively
questions.explanation: Ethos is built by demonstrating competence, honesty and good judgement — for example through relevant experience, reliable sources, and objectively addressing counterarguments. Interrupting or joking away difficult questions instead undermines credibility.

questions.prompt: A letter to the editor builds its entire argument on a single anecdote ("my neighbour lost his job, so immigration is bad for the economy"). What is the rhetorical weakness here?
questions.opener: Is a single example enough to substantiate a general claim?
choices: The anecdote is too emotional to count as an argument at all
A single example is generalised into a broad conclusion, without support from wider statistics or research
The anecdote contains too many numbers
The letter has the wrong kind of sender for the topic
questions.explanation: Drawing a general conclusion from a single example (hasty generalisation) makes the argument weak, since an anecdote does not show how representative it is. Emotion in itself does not disqualify an argument, but the lack of broader evidence does.

questions.prompt: A science journalist writes about the same research findings both in a specialist journal for experts and in an evening tabloid for the general public. What is typically adapted the most between the two texts?
questions.opener: What does one audience already know that the other does not?
choices: The research findings themselves, which must be changed depending on the target audience
Word choice, technical terminology, examples and the degree of background explanation are adapted to the audience's prior knowledge
Nothing needs to be adapted since facts should always be presented identically
Only the typeface in the printed text
questions.explanation: Good adaptation to the recipient means word choice, technical terms, examples and level of explanation are adjusted to the audience's prior knowledge — experts need less background and can handle more terminology than the general public. The factual content itself, however, should be the same in both texts.

questions.prompt: Analyse the following argument and identify the logical fallacy: "We know climate change is real because almost all scientists say so, and almost all scientists say so because climate change is real."
questions.opener: Look at what is used as evidence for the conclusion, and what is used as evidence for that evidence.
questions.answer: The argument is built on circular reasoning: the conclusion (climate change is real) is justified by a premise (scientists say so), and that premise is in turn justified by the very same conclusion it was meant to prove. The argument therefore provides no independent support for the claim, even though the conclusion itself may be true for other, independent reasons (e.g. actual measurement data and consensus studies).
steps: Identify what the conclusion of the argument is: that climate change is real.
Identify what is given as support (the premise): that almost all scientists say so.
Examine how the premise is in turn justified — here it turns out to be justified by the same conclusion.
Note that the reasoning goes in a circle and therefore provides no independent evidence.
Distinguish between the argument being flawed and whether the conclusion might still be true for other reasons.

questions.prompt: Summarise the most common logical fallacies, as well as what builds credibility and audience adaptation respectively.
questions.opener: Group them by what kind of "shortcut" the fallacy takes.
questions.answer: Ad hominem: attacks the person, not the argument · Straw man: distorts the opponent's position · False dichotomy: presents only two alternatives as the only possibilities · Circular reasoning: the conclusion is used as support for itself · Hasty generalisation: draws a broad conclusion from a single example · Ethos: built from competence, honesty and objectively addressing counterarguments · Audience adaptation: word choice, technical language and level of explanation are adjusted to the audience's prior knowledge, while the factual content remains the same.

questions.prompt: "If we allow students to have phones in the classroom, soon they'll want video games, then TVs, and eventually school will be an amusement park." What logical fallacy is this an example of?
questions.opener: The argument assumes a chain of ever-worse consequences without actually showing the chain is likely.
choices: Slippery slope
Ad hominem
Circular reasoning
Argument from authority
questions.explanation: A slippery slope argument claims that a first step will inevitably lead to a chain of increasingly extreme consequences, without actually showing that chain is likely. Here there is no evidence that phones in the classroom would lead to the claimed consequences.

questions.prompt: What is the logical fallacy called where one concludes that, because B happened after A, A must have caused B, without further support?
questions.opener: The name is Latin for "after this, therefore because of this".
choices: The post hoc fallacy
Straw man
False dichotomy
Ad hominem
questions.explanation: The post hoc fallacy mistakes temporal order for causation: just because B came after A does not automatically mean A caused B, without further evidence.

questions.prompt: What can undermine a speaker's ethos, even if the arguments themselves are correct?
questions.opener: Think about what happens to the audience's trust if the speaker has previously proven unreliable.
choices: Having previously been caught deliberately spreading falsehoods on the very same issue
Having relevant education in the subject
Referring to several independent sources
Addressing counterarguments objectively
questions.explanation: If a speaker has previously been caught deliberately lying on the same issue, their credibility (ethos) is seriously damaged, even if the current argument happens to be correct. Relevant education, source references, and objectively addressing counterarguments instead strengthen ethos.

questions.prompt: A government text about new regulations is rewritten into an easy-to-read version for a broader audience. What should primarily change?
questions.opener: Think about what should become easier to understand, and what should stay the same.
choices: Sentence length, word choice and the degree of technical language, while the factual content remains essentially the same
The actual regulations being described, so that they become less strict
Nothing needs to change at all
Only the typeface in the printed version
questions.explanation: An easy-to-read version adapts sentence length, word choice and the amount of technical language to the audience's prior knowledge, while the factual content — the regulations themselves — stays the same. Changing the actual regulations would mean the texts no longer describe the same reality.

questions.prompt: "If you care about children's safety, you must support this proposal." What is the problem with this reasoning?
questions.opener: Consider whether this is really the only way to show that you care about children's safety.
choices: It is an emotional appeal that bypasses the actual issue by linking a highly charged premise to a specific conclusion without genuine logical connection
It is circular reasoning
It is a false dichotomy between exactly two alternatives
It is an argument from authority
questions.explanation: The reasoning exploits an emotionally charged premise (children's safety) to force through a specific conclusion, without actually showing that this particular proposal is the only way to protect children's safety. It is therefore primarily an emotional appeal that bypasses the actual issue, rather than circular reasoning or a clear-cut false dichotomy.

questions.prompt: Which of the following most strengthens the credibility of an opinion piece on a complex topic?
questions.opener: Think about what shows the writer has an honest, nuanced relationship to the topic.
choices: Transparently stating sources and acknowledging the limitations of the underlying evidence
Avoiding mentioning any figures at all
Using as many superlatives as possible
Never mentioning that others might hold a different view
questions.explanation: Transparently stating sources and openly acknowledging any limitations in the underlying evidence shows honesty and strengthens credibility. Avoiding figures, overusing superlatives, or ignoring other viewpoints instead undermines trust.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to consider the sender's purpose when reading a text critically?
questions.opener: Think about how different purposes can affect which information is highlighted or selected.
choices: The purpose (e.g. to sell, persuade or inform) can affect how information is framed or selected
The sender's purpose is never relevant to how a text should be interpreted
All texts have exactly the same purpose: to be objective
The purpose is always clearly stated in the headline
questions.explanation: A sender's purpose, such as selling a product, persuading of an opinion, or informing factually, often affects which information is highlighted or left out. Being aware of the purpose helps the reader interpret the text more critically, and the purpose is rarely explicitly stated in the headline.
